interpretation: Theorem 1.1 presents single-value zeta evaluation as a resource tuple rather than as an arithmetic-operation exponent alone: accuracy t^-lambda costs t^(4/13) times polylogarithmic online operations, while precomputation and storage of the same power-law order are charged separately, and the operands have O_lambda((log t)^2) bits. This exposes the auxiliary resource burden instead of hiding it, but the span does not establish amortization or reuse across different t-values. The algorithm is modular at the Riemann-Siegel interface because it targets the main sum and does not depend on the precise remainder formula; this is an upper-bound and representation claim, not a lower bound, an RH result, or evidence that the unoptimized constants are practical.

The following prose derives bit complexity from operand size, notes that constants were not optimized, and says the methods exclusively compute the Riemann-Siegel main sum independently of the precise remainder function.

interpretation: The cubic descent is progressive only while its representation remains approximately closed: normalized coefficients, sufficient length, 1 <= bK, and the small-cubic condition allow repeated shortening into controlled linear combinations of cubic sums. The algorithm therefore treats failed invariants as routing decisions. A short sum is evaluated directly; failure of 1 <= bK gives a small-quadratic-coefficient regime where bounded phase derivatives support a short Euler-Maclaurin expansion; sole failure of cubic closure triggers exactly one further transform to a possibly high-degree sum of length roughly at most K^mu, evaluable in polylogarithmic time only with FFT data costing K^(4mu+o(1)) precomputation. This gains certified progress across incompatible regimes at the price of multiple evaluators and a costly terminal data structure. The overview only anticipates cheap computation of the nonstationary remainder R2; its proof remains elsewhere.
source_support: The span states the iteration conditions and resulting length reduction, then separately handles small K by direct evaluation and bK < 1 by Euler-Maclaurin using the displayed derivative control. It explains growth of the transformed cubic coefficient, applies one last transform when the small-cubic condition alone fails, and summarizes the resulting roughly K^mu high-degree sum and K^(4mu+o(1)) FFT precomputation. It explicitly describes efficient R2 treatment as anticipated rather than proved here.
nonparaphrase_operation: Extracts the case split as an adaptive stopping invariant: each way approximate cubic closure can fail selects a different certified continuation, clarifying why boundary exits are part of the complexity mechanism rather than exceptions to it.
speculation_status: The cases, conditions, cost orders, and deferred status of R2 are source-grounded. Describing them as adaptive routing is a supported conceptual interpretation; no proof-search claim is retained.
quality_reason: Accepted after deleting the imported formal-proof-search framing and distinguishing proved exit mechanisms from the overview's deferred claim about the nonstationary remainder.

interpretation: Lemma 5.4 turns a nonstationary cubic integral into finite local data by changing the contour rather than estimating the original oscillation directly. Cauchy deformation replaces the real y-segment by a finite slanted segment C1 and a vertical segment C2; x bounded away from zero together with small |c|K1^2 makes both transformed integrands decay at least at an exp(-y/6)-type rate. Consequently the long y-range can be discarded after truncation at L = ceil(6 nu), and subdivision plus Taylor expansion retains only O(nu^2) polynomial-moment integrals coupled to F(K; a+alpha x,b). The gain is a certified polylogarithmic-size representation; what is lost is direct access to the discarded tail, controlled only through the error bound. The lemma does not cover a stationary/near-zero-x regime, and the terminal evaluation of the displayed reduced integrals is delegated to the earlier treatment after (5.9).

interpretation: Lemma 5.6 certifies the external x-half-lines by composing two stability transformations. First, deforming the finite y-segment to C1/C2 creates exponential y-decay under the small-cubic hypothesis, enabling truncation and local Taylor reduction. Second, the x-half-line is rotated to C3 or C4 according to the sign of the quadratic coefficient. In the branch where the rotated integrand initially grows, the x-integral is written as a full-line Gaussian minus a negative half-line: the correction decays and is reduced through truncation, Taylor expansion, and incomplete-Gamma evaluation, while explicit Gaussian integration converts the bulk term into a short y-integral. Both routes end in the cited quadratic exponential sums handled by Theorem 2.1, so the displayed tail integrals require no additional terminal evaluator. This closure depends on all of the lemma's separation, coefficient, index-range, and smallness hypotheses; it does not establish an unrestricted contour rule.
source_support: The span deforms the y-contour to C1/C2, obtains exp(-y/16)-type decay, truncates and Taylor-expands to (5.38), and chooses C3 or C4 by the sign of alpha2. For positive alpha2 it derives a tau_k lower bound, splits the growing branch into a full Gaussian and negative-half-line correction, evaluates the latter via incomplete Gamma functions and the former via (5.46), and reduces both to the quadratic sums cited from Section 5 of Hia11 and handled by Theorem 2.1. The C2 route uses the analogous tilde-tau bound, and the negative external contour is treated as a conjugate case.
